transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington I'm Ryland Barton. Israeli Prime Minister
Benjamin Netanyahu says a pilot stabbed another pilot during a flight from the
United Arab Emirates to Israel and then apparently tried to crash the plane.
Passengers and crews subdued the attacker and the plane made a safe
emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. It's not clear what had motivated the attack.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says the U.S. military will cut 20% of its
generals and admirals. The ideological clowns are out. The patriotic cowboys are
in with testosterone testing on top. Diversity is not our strength. Unity is
our strength. Hegseth has targeted diversity programs, launched a review of
ground combat units with female troops, and added new screening programs for
what he calls testosterone deficiency among male personnel. He made the speech
to junior officers and enlisted leaders today, focusing on how he has drastically
retooled the military by targeting what he calls "woke culture." The U.S. military
has completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a
12-year mission against the Islamic State group. President Trump hailed the
withdrawal as a victory for the U.S. and Iraq. This orderly departure of coalition
forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base marks the end of a very expensive
excursion into hell. Concerns remain about the resurgence of the Islamic State
group in attacks by Iran-linked groups, the future of Iraqi militias, and also
remains uncertain as the government seeks to disarm them. NPR has learned of
a plan for a massive new data center on federal land in Utah. As NPR's Jeff
Brumfield reports, it would involve building hundreds of nuclear reactors.
The proposal seen by NPR came from the company Valor Atomics. Valor already has
a test reactor operating in Utah, but it wants to build around 450 more small
nuclear reactors on 9,000 acres of federal land. The reactors would provide
power for data centers, among other things. Neil Clark with the Southern Utah
Wilderness Alliance says Valor isn't the only company quietly seeking to build
data centers on public lands. It's pretty obvious that they're trying to keep
these proposals and these processes totally under the radar to make sure the
public is kept in the dark. The Bureau of Land Management says the public will
have an opportunity to comment on the proposal after the agency reviews the
application for completeness. Jeff Brumfield, NPR News. An internal watchdog
at the Federal Reserve finds poor management contributed to cost overruns
on the central bank's headquarters renovation, but the inspector general
finds no deliberate misconduct or criminal wrongdoing. The Trump
administration had launched a criminal probe of the building project as
President Trump pressured former Fed Chair Jerome Powell to lower interest
rates. The federal judge pulled the plug on that investigation back in March,
finding it was part of an improper pressure campaign. Most U.S. stocks fell
today. This is NPR News from Washington. A judge has ruled that the U.S. can
deport the Palestinian-born leader of Wisconsin's largest mosque on national
security grounds. Sarsour is a legal resident of the U.S. who's spoken out
against Israel. The Trump administration has wanted to remove Sarsour, Sarsour
since his arrest by ICE in March. It argues decades-old terrorism convictions
in Israel make him a threat to national security. Carnegie Mellon University has
now gotten the largest single donation in the history of higher education in
the U.S., three billion dollars, NPR's Janaki Mehta reports. The historic
donation comes from Kenneth Griffin, a hedge fund executive. A billion dollars
of that money will go toward Carnegie Mellon's Pittsburgh campus, including its
School of Computer Science, which will be named for Griffin. The other two billion
dollars will go toward a campus in Miami where the university says 3,500 students
are expected to start enrolling in 2028. University also says it will "invert
the higher education model." Instead of organizing by traditional academic
majors, it plans to instead organize learning around societal challenges like
human health, climate resilience, and national security. This comes as many
higher education institutions around the country are shrinking because of
enrollment and other challenges. Janaki Mehta, NPR News. A huge gray shark named
Bukhangi has become an honorary mascot in South Korea's biggest port city, Busan.
The shark has become a social media sensation, but guiding it back to open
water has proved tricky. Five vessels were deployed yesterday, but the crews
gave up after hours unsuccessfully spraying streams of water to herd the
shark toward the open sea. This is NPR News.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announces U.S. military will cut 20% of generals and admirals, targets diversity programs
U.S. military completes withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending 12-year mission against Islamic State
Company Valor Atomics proposes building 450 small nuclear reactors on 9,000 acres of federal land in Utah
Federal Reserve inspector general finds poor management in headquarters renovation but no deliberate misconduct or criminal wrongdoing
U.S. stocks fall on market today
Judge rules U.S. can deport Palestinian-born Wisconsin mosque leader on national security grounds
Kenneth Griffin donates three billion dollars to Carnegie Mellon University, largest single donation in higher education history
Gray shark Bukhangi becomes social media sensation in South Korea's Busan port city; efforts to herd to sea unsuccessful
